title: Five saloks
hookLine: Kabir's couplets are short enough to carry in the pocket (ang 1364–1377)

lines: A STICKY NOTE ON THE FRIDGE.
cards: A sticky note on the fridge. A line written on the back of a hand before an exam. A phrase a grandmother said so often the whole family can finish it.
Some words are built to travel light. Kabir's saloks are like that: short couplets, signed with his name at the start, filling the pages of the Guru Granth Sahib from Ang 1364 to 1377.
Today, five of them, turned over one at a time.

teach.h: DO IT TODAY; DO IT NOW.
teach.b: All five in paraphrase. The first is about time: Kabir, what you'd do tomorrow, do today; what you'd do today, do now. Later there'll be nothing to do, once death is standing over you.
Short enough to say in a doorway, and it stings. The second is about this life.

teach.h: RIPE FRUIT DOESN'T RETURN TO THE BRANCH.
teach.b: A human birth is hard to come by, Kabir says, and it doesn't come again and again: like ripe fruit fallen in the forest, it never goes back onto the branch. The third is a little map.
Where there is wisdom, there is dharma, right living. Where there is falsehood, there is sin. Where there is greed, there is death.

teach.h: WHERE FORGIVENESS IS, THE LORD IS.
teach.b: And where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself. The line ends not on a rule, but on forgiveness, with God standing in it. The fourth is a chain, across several couplets.
Become a pebble on the path and drop your pride.
Then he catches himself: a pebble still hurts a traveler's foot, so become dust. But dust blows up and soils the body, so become water. But water turns cold and hot, so become like the Lord.
Each picture is corrected by the next: humility that keeps checking itself. The fifth is for the end of the day.
Kabir, nothing in me is mine; whatever there is, is Yours. If I hand back to You what's Yours, what does it cost me? That's what a salok can do: turn one ordinary thought until your grip loosens.
They're built to be learned by heart, so they're there in the doorway when you need them.

how: Kabir's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many Sikhs learn favorite couplets by heart and quote them in conversation.

o: five promises Kabir made before Maghar
five long hymns Kabir sang in a single raag
Kabir's short couplets, signed with his name

p: never goes back onto the branch

s: Kabir's saloks open with his name, like a signature
his couplets begin 'Kabir', then say their piece.
the pebble salok ends with becoming dust
dust soils the body, water turns hot and cold; the chain ends with becoming like the Lord.
the salok on wisdom and greed ends on a rule
it ends on forgiveness: where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself.

games.q: Kabir has said: become a pebble on the path and drop your pride. but a pebble still hurts a traveler's foot. what does he say next?
o: stay a pebble, but a smooth one.
games.why: become dust, he says, and then corrects that too: dust soils the body, so become water; water turns hot and cold, so become like the Lord.

practice: Pick the salok that caught on something in you: do it now, the ripe fruit, forgiveness, the pebble, or nothing is mine.
Say it to yourself slowly, in your own words, again and again, letting it get shorter each time until it fits in one breath. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as the breath goes out.

wordCard.voice: Five saloks. Kabir's short couplets, signed with his name: do it now, the ripe fruit, forgiveness, the pebble, and nothing is mine.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a short verse or couplet; Kabir's in the Granth run from Ang 1364 to 1377.

carryVoice: Your line: short and sharp. A few words can hold a whole teaching. That's day seven hundred fifty-nine.
